newsitem.title: NEW ZEALAND: OPINION-From the Beehive-Tortuous coalition talks.
newsitem.headline: OPINION-From the Beehive-Tortuous coalition talks.

text.p: WELLINGTON, Nov 12 - Political pressure on the "big three" to accelerate negotiations on a new coalition government is mounting - despite insistence by New Zealand First that it needs more time to nail down a deal.
Some reports suggest that senior figures in NZ First show no signs of being ruffled by the impatience of its negotiating partners.
Yet, NZ First leader Winston Peters bites back at journalists who see the process as unnecessarily complicated.

NZ First's objective is a line-by-line commitment in an extraordinarily detailed policy contract, rather than broad agreement on a policy path that might be followed, with deviations as and when dictated by events.
The difficulty is that in seeking to settle major policy within the confines of the coalition negotiating room, NZ First has first had to define what its own policy meant.
Many of its policy ideas, floated off, it seems, without undue analysis during the election campaign, could turn out to be potential landmines for current monetary and fiscal policy.

Ironically, the political uncertainty recognised as endemic to the MMP electoral system and predicted to send the financial markets into a tailspin has in fact had the opposite effect: the markets are thriving, the New Zealand exchange rate has hardened, and billions of dollars in foreign funds have poured into the country.
In contrast, both the export sector and the domestic economy are being hit in a way neither expected.
Reports from the retail sector suggest that a week after the election, the New Zealand consumer buttoned up the purse and virtually stopped spending.

And exporters who had expected an easing in interest rates that would in turn lead to a falling exchange rate have been dismayed to find overseas investors regard the New Zealand dollar as one-way bet.
Now Reserve Bank Governor Don Brash has had to warn the politicians -- who may be concerned to alleviate the pressure on the export sector -- against what he termed "unconventional" measures.
"Whether those measures involved acceptance of 'temporarily' higher inflation or specific regulatory or tax-related measures, the longer-run consequences would be just as unhealthy," Brash said.
Just what hints Brash has caught of "unconventional" measures he did not specify, but there is little doubt the politicians are in a severe bind.
On one side, Brash is calling for potential coalition partners to drop the second round of tax cuts if there is to be any net increase in government spending.
On the other side, Winston Peters' fiscal priorities call for a minimum of $750 million additional spending.
As Brash delicately puts it, "there is obviously a huge problem for political leaders in this situation".
Those politicians who campaigned so strongly against foreign investment in the run-up to the election are now in danger of becoming prisoners to it.
The capital inflows will only be shut off if the politicians do something stupid -- but if they take that kind of action, they risk their own political future.

Labour's finance spokesman Michael Cullen suggests "a little uncertainty" in the financial markets would go a long way to ensuring that the unjustified and unsustainable rise in the New Zealand dollar over the last few weeks is reversed.
The process of injecting "a little uncertainty" into financial markets always risks an epidemic of uncertainty that turns out to be a crisis.
Finance Minister Bill Birch argues that it is the additional government spending advocated by Cullen that is creating the tensions over monetary policy and the exchange rate.
Before the election, Winston Peters was quoted as saying that he wanted to go to his party's annual convention next year, look his supporters in the eye, and tell them "we held the line".
But just which line?
Note - The opinions expressed in this article are those of the writer and should not be attributed to Reuters.
